title: Update on Femtosecond Laser-Assisted Cataract Surgery: A Review
condition_or_topic: Femtosecond laser-assisted cataract and lens surgery (FLACS)
clinical_background: Cataract surgery increasingly aims to meet refractive goals as well as remove an opaque lens. Preoperative selection of intraocular lens (IOL) power and design, particularly for premium IOLs, places greater demands on surgical precision and predictability. FLACS was developed to improve the reproducibility and customization of steps traditionally performed during conventional phacoemulsification, including capsulotomy, lens fragmentation, and corneal incisions. Femtosecond laser systems use different pulse-energy patterns, which may affect their clinical benefits and limitations.
objectives: Review current evidence on the effectiveness and safety of FLACS by examining its surgical outcomes and complications.
Assess the reported advantages and limitations of high- and low-energy femtosecond laser pulses.
study_design: Review of current evidence on the effectiveness, safety, outcomes, and complications of femtosecond laser-assisted cataract (lens) surgery, including high- and low-energy pulse techniques.
interventions: Femtosecond laser-assisted cataract surgery (FLACS) using high-energy pulses
Femtosecond laser-assisted cataract surgery (FLACS) using low-energy pulses
main_conclusion: The authors conclude that FLACS has complication and adverse-event rates comparable to CP when differences between laser pulse types are considered. It may offer mid-term visual advantages and particular value in complex eyes or surgery involving premium IOLs, but its higher cost keeps CP the standard cataract technique.
narrative_summary:
This review examines the effectiveness, safety, indications and limitations of femtosecond laser-assisted cataract surgery (FLACS), with particular attention to differences between high- and low-energy laser pulses. Compared with conventional phacoemulsification (CP), FLACS offers more precise and reproducible capsulotomy and can reduce the phacoemulsification energy delivered by 33–70% through laser lens fragmentation. Laser-created corneal and arcuate incisions also permit greater control of their dimensions and placement. Some reviews report better mid-term visual acuity with FLACS, although the reported difference is less than 0.05 logMAR and is not clinically significant; long-term visual and refractive superiority remains unclear.

The authors distinguish complications associated mainly with high-energy pulses, particularly pupil constriction and anterior capsule tears or tags, from findings with low-energy FLACS, for which recent reports describe near absence of laser-induced miosis and capsule complication rates comparable to CP. FLACS may be useful when precise IOL positioning is especially important or in eyes with dense cataracts, zonular instability, corneal dystrophy or macular vulnerability. Suitability remains constrained by docking and imaging requirements, inadequate pupillary dilation and some cataract characteristics. Evidence specific to premium IOL subgroups and comparisons among laser systems is limited. Equipment and consumable costs make FLACS less cost-effective than CP, which remains the standard approach.
interpretation: The review concludes that FLACS is non-inferior to CP for complication and adverse-event rates when differences between laser pulse patterns are considered. FLACS provides more precise and customizable capsulotomy and may offer a mid-term visual advantage, although a statistically significant visual-acuity difference reported in some reviews was not clinically significant (inferior to 0.05 logMAR). Evidence suggests that low-energy FLACS has few anterior capsule complications and almost no laser-induced miosis, with rates comparable to CP; these findings do not apply to high-energy FLACS. FLACS may be safer in selected complex eyes, but its greater cost prevents it from replacing CP as the standard cataract-surgery technique.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Earlier accounts commonly treated laser-induced miosis and anterior capsule complications as general drawbacks of FLACS without separating high- from low-energy systems. More recent low-energy evidence challenges that generalization, whereas high-energy FLACS remains associated with pupil constriction and more anterior capsule complications. Several studies found no statistically significant long-term differences between FLACS and CP in visual acuity or refractive outcomes; some reviews found a mid-term visual-acuity advantage that was statistically, but not clinically, significant. Evidence on refractive predictability differs by review design and follow-up. Although most studies reported more posterior capsule opacification after FLACS, reported Nd: YAG capsulotomy rates were lower than after CP. Reviews and meta-analyses reported less endothelial cell loss with FLACS, while recent adequately powered randomized trials in normal eyes found no statistically significant difference. Most reviews found no significant difference in cystoid macular edema.
clinical_implications: Capsulotomy precision and centration may be particularly important for the performance of toric, enhanced-depth-of-focus, or multifocal IOLs.

Reduced phacoemulsification energy with FLACS may benefit eyes with hard cataracts, endothelial disease, or other surgical vulnerabilities; the review also identifies lens subluxation, zonular instability, and macular vulnerability as settings in which FLACS may be safer.
Pulse energy affects the clinical interpretation of FLACS safety: low-energy systems appear to avoid much of the miosis and anterior capsule complication burden associated with high-energy systems.

FSAK offers more predictable correction than manual keratotomy, but its correction range is limited to low levels of corneal astigmatism. Most available studies favor toric IOLs over FSAK for moderate-to-high (>1.25 D), against-the-rule, or limbus-to-limbus astigmatism.
Platform acquisition and consumables make FLACS less cost-effective than CP; an FS laser also does not eliminate the need for a phacoemulsification/aspiration device.
Most FS platforms require patient transfer after laser treatment, increasing overall procedure time; the portable platform can avoid that transfer and permit surgical durations comparable to CP.
practice_implications: Consider FLACS for refractive cataract or lens surgery involving premium IOLs, and for selected hard cataracts or complex eyes in which its capsulotomy or lens-fragmentation characteristics may help.
Use the distinctions between low- and high-energy laser systems when planning surgery and assessing the risk of pupil constriction or capsule complications.
Consider FSAK for low levels of corneal astigmatism; its incision depth, location, and axis can be planned, and an anterior penetrating incision can be opened to increase its effect.

Assess whether ocular anatomy permits docking and whether anterior-segment imaging is adequate before using FLACS. Poor dilation and specified prior corneal or glaucoma procedures may present additional challenges rather than absolute contraindications.

Do not advise laser lens fragmentation for white cataracts because opaque tissue makes adequate imaging difficult. The review distinguishes the additional risk in intumescent cataracts on platforms that perform capsulotomy before fragmentation from platforms using the reverse sequence.

For poor pupillary dilation, the review describes preoperative topical medications, intracameral agents, viscomydriasis, and iris expansion devices as possible approaches; high-energy FLACS may require additional measures against laser-induced miosis.

For prevention of laser-associated miosis, observe laser-treatment duration and the recommended distance between the intended capsulotomy edge and the pupillary margin (>1 mm recommended). Pre-operative NSAIDs alone are normally insufficient to prevent this complication.
If suction is lost, suspend laser treatment immediately to avoid mistreatment.
Where peripheral corneal vascularization interferes with a laser incision, seek a less vascularized site if possible when setting the cut.
limitations: Most published FLACS studies do not provide subgroup analyses by the type of IOL implanted, limiting assessment in premium-IOL surgery.
Published comparisons seldom distinguish high- from low-energy pulses; subgroup evidence for posterior capsule opacification by pulse energy is almost inexistent.
Most published studies do not grade posterior capsule opacification, limiting interpretation of its effect on vision and of the reported Nd: YAG capsulotomy rates.
Patient-reported outcome evidence is scarce, and variation in assessment methods and measures hinders comparison between FLACS and CP.
Nomograms developed specifically for femtosecond laser-created arcuate incisions are scarce.
open_questions: Whether the possible visual benefits of FLACS extend to toric or presbyopia lens surgery remains uncertain.
The full clinical significance of differences between low- and high-energy FS technologies has not yet been established.
Further evidence is needed to clarify posterior capsule opacification by pulse-energy subgroup and its relation to Nd: YAG capsulotomy and visual outcomes.
future_directions: Conduct larger studies that assess the different laser systems and pulse-energy patterns.
Include analyses by implanted IOL type to evaluate FLACS in premium-IOL surgery.
Develop more comprehensive and standardized PROMs for rigorous assessment of patient-reported outcomes.

main_findings.description: The studies reviewed found femtosecond laser-assisted capsulotomy more precise, predictable, reproducible and well centered than manual capsulorhexis.
main_findings.context: Capsulotomy dimensions and centration can affect IOL position and postoperative refraction.

main_findings.description: Some cited studies found better IOL centration after FSL capsulotomy than after manual capsulorhexis.
main_findings.context: The finding is attributed to cited studies, not to a new comparison conducted by this review.

main_findings.description: Some authors reported more favorable capsule-IOL overlap when capsulotomy was centered on the capsular bag rather than the pupil.
main_findings.context: Anterior capsule overlap across 360 degrees of the IOL anterior surface is associated with less posterior capsule opacification.

main_findings.description: The reviewed evidence associates laser lens fragmentation with less phacoemulsification energy than CP.
main_findings.metric: reduction in phacoemulsification energy with FLACS versus CP
main_findings.context: The authors attribute the reduction to lens softening before phacoemulsification.

main_findings.description: Compared with manually constructed corneal incisions, laser-created incisions were reported to have less wound gape and edema, with less susceptibility to leakage and more predictable surgically induced astigmatism.
main_findings.context: The cited studies also describe laser-created wounds as stable and repeatable.

main_findings.description: FSAK was described as more predictable and repeatable than manual keratotomy for corneal astigmatism correction.
main_findings.context: Laser settings allow control of incision depth and location, including entirely intrastromal incisions.

main_findings.description: Several cited studies found comparable safety, efficacy and stability for FS laser-assisted corneal incisions and toric IOLs when correcting mild, central, with-the-rule astigmatism.
main_findings.context: The comparison concerns the specified mild astigmatism subgroup.

main_findings.description: Most studies reviewed favored toric IOL implantation over FSAK for correction of moderate-to-high, against-the-rule or limbus-to-limbus astigmatism.
main_findings.context: The stated superiority is limited to the specified astigmatism patterns or magnitude.

main_findings.description: Several studies found no statistically significant long-term difference between FLACS and CP in corrected or uncorrected distance visual acuity or refractive outcomes.
main_findings.context: The review reports no numerical effect estimates for these long-term comparisons.

main_findings.description: Some cited systematic reviews and meta-analyses found statistically better medium-term corrected and uncorrected visual acuity with FLACS, but the difference was not clinically significant.
main_findings.context: The comparison was FLACS versus CP at medium-term follow-up.

main_findings.description: Kranitz et al found significantly greater IOL decentration and worse CDVA with CP than with FLACS.
Reddy et al reported greater IOL decentration after CP than after FLACS.
Large reviews based on RCTs indicated greater short-term refractive predictability with FLACS than with CP, but no long-term advantage.
main_findings.context: The review describes the evidence on postoperative SE and MAE as dependent on which trials were included.

main_findings.description: Reviews including a small number of RCTs reported an MAE advantage for FLACS over CP.
main_findings.context: Finding from cited reviews; other reviews did not establish a consistent long-term advantage.

main_findings.description: Systematic reviews combining prospective and retrospective trials found a clinically important MAE difference only at mid-term follow-up.

For surgically induced astigmatism, the clinically relevant difference between FLACS and CP appears to concern predictability rather than overall magnitude; the latter did not differ statistically significantly.
main_findings.context: Predictability refers to achieved versus attempted correction.

main_findings.description: The reviewed evidence favors FLACS over CP for effective phacoemulsification time, cumulative dissipated energy and capsulotomy circularity.
main_findings.context: More precise and reproducible circularity may improve lens centration and reduce the risk of lens malposition.

main_findings.description: Some cited studies reported less capsular bag shrinkage with FLACS than with CP, a factor relevant to subsequent IOL tilt and decentration.
main_findings.context: The review states that capsular bag shrinkage is more prominent after CP.

notable_adverse_events: Docking for FLACS can cause transient conjunctival redness or hemorrhage; incomplete laser treatment after suction loss is described as very rare.
Subconjunctival hemorrhage with FLACS is reported more often with applanation docking than with a liquid interface.
Anterior capsular tears or tags after FLACS were reported at rates ranging from 0.1% to as high as 4%; the review relates much of this variation to high-energy pulse platforms.
Recent cited studies report fewer anterior capsular tears or tags with low-energy than with high-energy pulse FLACS; the incidence with low-energy FLACS is described as comparable to CP.
Posterior capsule rupture is reported less frequently with FLACS than with CP.
Capsular block syndrome followed by posterior capsule rupture is described as extremely rare during high-energy laser lens fragmentation and is not reported with low-energy FLACS.

High-energy pulse FLACS is associated with laser-induced pupil constriction almost universally in the literature discussed. Recent publications and the few reviews with a low-energy subgroup report virtually no laser-induced miosis with low-energy FLACS, at a frequency comparable to CP.

Most cited studies report a higher incidence of posterior capsule opacification after FLACS than after CP, although other cited reports describe less frequent long-term capsular bag-IOL events after FLACS. The review notes that PCO subgroup evidence by pulse energy is almost nonexistent.

Nd: YAG capsulotomy rates are reportedly lower after FLACS than after CP despite reports of more posterior capsule opacification. The suggested explanation of a lower PCO grade is not established because grading is absent from most reports.

Well-powered RCTs in normal eyes did not find a statistically significant difference in endothelial cell loss between FLACS and CP, whereas several reviews and meta-analyses reported less endothelial cell loss with FLACS.
Most cited systematic reviews and meta-analyses found no significant difference in cystoid macular edema incidence between FLACS and CP.

The overall consequences of capsule-related complications did not appear statistically significantly different between FLACS and CP in global comparisons; the review cautions that such complications can compromise premium IOL implantation.
The incidence of Descemet’s membrane detachment, endothelial misalignment and posterior wound contraction is described as low with FLACS.
FSAK is associated in the reviewed literature with less irritation, epithelial ingrowth, loss of corneal sensation and infection risk.
The review reports that intraoperative complication rates decrease significantly in most studies after an estimated minimum learning curve of 100–200 cases, depending on surgeon experience.

subgroup_analyses: Low-energy, high-frequency pulses are described as producing less gas and collateral tissue damage than high-energy, low-frequency pulses; lower-energy capsulotomy produces smoother edges and fewer reported capsular complications.

Reports of pupil constriction commonly concern high-energy FLACS or do not separate pulse types. Publications assessing low-energy FLACS report pupil behavior comparable to CP, rather than the miosis associated with high-energy FLACS.

For white cataracts, the reviewed evidence distinguishes platforms by surgical sequence: performing lens fragmentation before capsulotomy can equalize capsular bag pressure and help prevent Argentinian Flag Syndrome; fragmentation after capsulotomy presents an additional posterior capsule risk in intumescent cataracts.
Laser-assisted fragmentation reduces phacoemulsification time, irrigation volume and EPT particularly in harder cataracts; the review associates these reductions with less endothelial cell loss.
Studies of corneal dystrophies, including Fuchs’, provide evidence of an endothelial protective effect of FLACS through reduced phacoemulsification exposure.

Some studies involving patients with AMD reported lower central macular volume shortly after FLACS than after CP. The review considers a possible advantage in eyes with macular vulnerability but does not report a general retinal advantage.
Most retinal measurements discussed, including total macular volume, foveal thickness and the outer macular ring, were comparable between FLACS and CP.
Studies of patients receiving premium IOLs rarely report outcomes separately by implanted IOL type, limiting assessment of FLACS in that subgroup.
The review reports that pulse-energy-specific subgroup analyses of posterior capsule opacification are almost nonexistent.
secondary_results: Docking adds time relative to CP. Most FS platforms also require transfer after laser treatment, extending overall surgery; a portable platform permits surgical durations comparable to CP.

Capsulotomy regularity did not differ between applanation and liquid docking interfaces in the literature cited, although applanation interfaces have some evidence of more anterior capsular tears or tags associated with corneal folds.
Nonapplanating docking interfaces are described as inducing less intraocular pressure, providing a larger treatment area and accommodating lens tilt more effectively than applanation interfaces.
Patient-reported outcomes are sparsely studied, and differences between FLACS and CP cannot be assessed reliably across the heterogeneous measures used.

FLACS is described as less cost-effective than CP because of equipment and consumable costs; a phacoemulsification/aspiration device remains necessary to complete lens removal and capsular bag polishing.

diseases_and_conditions.context: Laser fragmentation may reduce phacoemulsification exposure and endothelial injury.

diseases_and_conditions.context: A complex surgical circumstance for which FLACS may reduce stress on ocular structures.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Femtosecond laser-assisted cataract surgery (FLACS) was developed to improve on conventional phacoemulsification through greater reproducibility, precision, accuracy, and customization. Its principal applications are capsulotomy, corneal incisions, lens fragmentation, and arcuate incisions. These capabilities matter particularly when patients seek better refractive outcomes and less dependence on spectacles, including when toric, enhanced depth-of-focus, or multifocal intraocular lenses are implanted. This review examines the effectiveness, safety, outcomes, complications, advantages, and limitations of high- and low-energy femtosecond laser pulses.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Modern cataract surgery includes implantation of an intraocular lens (IOL) whose power and design are selected after preoperative assessment. Efforts to improve postoperative refraction, including advances in biometry formulas, have made cataract surgery increasingly refractive in purpose. Cataract removal and elective refractive lens surgery share their essential steps and can be viewed along a continuum of patient needs. A patient's informed decision and perceived independence influence whether to operate on a cataract, regardless of its maturity; at the elective end of the continuum, freedom from spectacles is the principal aim. Rising expectations have encouraged new techniques and IOLs. FLACS arose as a potential means of improving efficacy and safety. The demonstrated precision and reproducibility of laser-assisted capsulotomy prompted extension of the technology to lens fragmentation and corneal incisions. Because premium IOLs demand predictable, accurate surgery, this review updates the evidence on FLACS outcomes, effectiveness, and safety.

document_sections.heading: Technology Femtosecond Lasers
document_sections.content: Femtosecond lasers produce pulses lasting on the order of 10−15 s. Their near-infrared output at 1053 nm creates tissue photodisruption while avoiding effects such as the thermal injury associated with earlier lasers. Power, repetition rate, and spot size permit further adjustment of the laser–tissue interaction. Photodisruption proceeds through plasma formation, shock-wave generation, and cavitation. Tissue separation occurs through ablation and cleaving, with pulse energy chiefly determining their relative contributions. The threshold for photodisruption varies with tissue characteristics, numerical aperture (NA), and wavelength. Higher-energy pulses produce more tissue ablation through expanding gas bubbles; lower-energy pulses ablate less tissue and rely more on cleaving, requiring higher frequencies and closer spot spacing.

document_sections.heading: Types of Femtosecond Laser Pulse
document_sections.content: Available pulse patterns comprise high-energy, low-frequency output on the order of µJ and KHz, used by most systems, and low-energy, high-frequency output in the range of nJ and MHz, produced by another platform. Low-energy pulses delivered at high repetition rates permit accurate focusing and precise cuts, generate less gas, and cause less collateral tissue damage. High-energy pulses exert substantially greater mechanical force on nearby tissue. At a given wavelength, pulse energy depends on focal spot size, which decreases as the NA of the focusing optics increases. NA can be increased by enlarging the focusing lens or bringing the optics nearer the eye. LenSx, VICTUS, Catalys, and LensAR use the former approach and require relatively stationary platforms with large optics. Femto LDV Z8 uses the latter: an articulated mirror arm directs the beam to a handpiece containing the focusing optics. This arrangement lowers pulse energy by a factor of 10 or more and permits use beneath a surgical microscope in a more compact, portable system.

document_sections.heading: Delivery Procedure
document_sections.content: Laser delivery requires a stable, tolerable patient interface. Docking uses either eye applanation with a curved lens or a liquid interface. Published evidence finds no difference in capsulotomy regularity between them, although corneal folds with applanation may increase anterior capsular tears or tags. Nonapplanating systems use a scleral suction ring and fluid chamber; their reported features include less induced intraocular pressure, a larger treatment area, and better accommodation of lens tilt. Docking adds time compared with conventional phacoemulsification (CP). Possible complications range from relatively frequent transient conjunctival redness or hemorrhage to very rare incomplete laser treatment after suction loss.

document_sections.heading: Supporting Imaging Technology
document_sections.content: Laser-assisted capsulotomy, corneal incisions, and lens fragmentation depend on reliable three-dimensional imaging of anterior eye structures. Most platforms use optical coherence tomography; LensAR uses 3D confocal structured illumination together with Scheimpflug imaging. Most systems also incorporate a camera for a frontal view of the eye.

document_sections.heading: Capsulotomy
document_sections.content: Capsulotomy shape and size affect effective lens position and, consequently, postoperative refraction. Incorrect sizing can contribute to IOL tilt, decentration, and greater posterior capsule opacification. Accurate centration is especially important for toric, enhanced-depth-of-focus, and multifocal IOLs. Studies have demonstrated greater precision, predictability, and reproducibility with femtosecond laser capsulotomy than with CP. Most platforms create the capsulotomy before fragmenting the lens, whereas Ziemer’s performs it afterward. In white cataracts, which are generally unsuitable for laser treatment on most platforms, fragmentation before capsular opening can equalize pressure within the bag and prevent Argentinian Flag Syndrome. Imaging during docking permits adjustment of capsulotomy diameter, centration, and usually the safety margin from the iris. Some studies found six-fold better IOL centration with laser capsulotomy than with manual capsulorrhexis. Available centration references include the pupil, corneal optical center, capsule center, lens apex, and first Purkinje reflex; platforms offer at least two such options. Some authors reported better capsule–IOL overlap with centration on the capsular bag rather than the pupil. Anterior capsule overlap around 360 degrees of the IOL anterior surface is generally associated with less posterior capsule opacification. A preoperative pupil diameter not inferior to 4 mm is normally compatible with available devices. Miosis after laser pretreatment has often been reported, but most publications examine high-energy FLACS or do not separate results by pulse energy. Recent low-energy FLACS literature finds pupil behavior comparable to CP without evidence of laser-induced miosis, potentially because less tissue disturbance produces less prostaglandin release. Applanation itself has also been described as reducing pupil size through transient ischemia of the iris sphincter. Measures used against miosis with high-energy systems include intracameral viscoelastic, injected or perfused epinephrine, and mechanical dilation. Capsulotomy energy influences anterior capsule strength and edge morphology. Some microscopy studies found manual capsulorhexis stronger than laser capsulotomy; higher-energy pulses produce more irregular edges, whereas lower-energy pulses produce smoother ones. Recent studies report fewer capsular tears or tags with low-energy than high-energy FLACS. Although diameter is adjustable, 5–5.25 mm is commonly selected; pupil dilation and device-specific safety margins may constrain it. Overall, laser capsulotomies are more accurate in size and shape, more reproducible, and better centered than manual capsulorhexis. Maintaining dilation and the considerable rate of capsule-related complications remain limitations associated with high-energy laser treatment.

document_sections.heading: Lens Fragmentation
document_sections.content: Femtosecond lasers fragment the lens nucleus in place of the corresponding ultrasound-based step of CP. Platforms offer different fragmentation patterns and adjustable anterior and posterior safety margins guided by capsular-bag imaging. Laser pretreatment shortens phacoemulsification time and cumulative dissipated energy (CDE), reducing exposure to ultrasound-associated oxidative stress, heat, inflammation, and tissue injury. Capsular block syndrome followed by posterior capsule rupture is extremely rare and occurs when gas bubbles from high-energy ablation create excessive pressure inside the bag. This event has not been reported with low-energy FLACS, which separates tissue predominantly by cleaving. By softening the lens, FLACS reduces delivered phacoemulsification energy by 33–70% compared with CP. Safe laser completion nevertheless requires adequate pupil dilation, and high-energy FLACS is contraindicated for white cataracts.

document_sections.heading: Corneal Incisions
document_sections.content: Femtosecond lasers permit customization of full-thickness corneal incision width, length, depth, shape, and position. Studies comparing laser and manual incisions report stable, reproducible, safe wounds, with less wound gape and edema after laser creation. Imaging-guided platform settings are used for both the principal incision and paracentesis. Compared with CP, the laser creates complex biplanar or triplanar wounds more consistently. Descemet’s membrane detachment, endothelial misalignment, and posterior wound contraction have low reported incidence with FLACS. Peripheral corneal vascularization can prevent completion of a laser cut because suction blanches limbal vessels, making manual assistance necessary; a less vascularized site should be selected where possible. Laser incisions are less susceptible to gape and leakage and offer more predictable surgically induced astigmatism, although wound location and completion remain limitations in some cases.

document_sections.heading: Arcuate Keratotomy
document_sections.content: Partial-thickness corneal incisions can correct corneal astigmatism. Compared with blade keratotomy, femtosecond laser treatment is more predictable and repeatable and can create fully intrastromal as well as anterior-penetrating arcuate incisions (AIs). The surgeon can specify their depth, length, position, and axis. Anterior-penetrating AIs can also be opened manually during or after surgery to increase their effect. Femtosecond laser-assisted arcuate keratotomy (FSAK) is associated with less irritation, epithelial ingrowth, and loss of corneal sensation, as well as lower infection risk; it can therefore be used in ocular surface disease or after keratoplasty. Intrastromal AIs are believed to produce less astigmatic correction than anterior-penetrating AIs because they spare Bowman’s membrane. Intrastromal cuts can also mark the implantation axis of toric IOLs without a refractive purpose. Several studies found comparable safety, efficacy, and stability between laser-assisted corneal incisions and toric IOL implantation for mild (<1.25 D), central, with-the-rule astigmatism. Most available studies favor toric IOLs over FSAK for moderate-to-high (>1.25 D), against-the-rule, or limbus-to-limbus astigmatism. Few femtosecond AI nomograms have been published. Wortz & Gupta developed one for low astigmatism. Baharozian et al’s anterior-penetrating laser AI nomogram targets <1.25 D, modifies Donnenfeld’s manual LRI nomogram, accounts for posterior corneal astigmatism according to astigmatism type, and uses a 9.0 mm optical zone. Relative to manual keratotomy, FSAK affords more accurate control of treatment depth and position. Intrastromal incisions are an additional laser-specific option, and opening laser-created incisions at the slit lamp permits postoperative adjustment. The correctable range remains limited to low corneal astigmatism, and better FSAK-specific nomograms are still needed.

document_sections.heading: Refractive and Visual Outcomes
document_sections.content: Several studies found no statistically significant long-term differences between FLACS and CP in corrected or uncorrected distance visual acuity or refractive outcomes. Some systematic reviews and meta-analyses reported statistically better medium-term corrected and uncorrected acuity with FLACS, but the difference was not clinically meaningful because it was inferior to 0.05 logMAR. Long-term acuity can be influenced by IOL tilt, decentration, and posterior capsule opacification; some reports describe these events as less frequent after FLACS. Capsular-bag shrinkage is an important contributor to later tilt and decentration and is more pronounced with CP. IOL position affects effective lens position, IOL power calculations, refraction, and the performance of toric, EDOF, and multifocal lenses. Kranitz et al found significantly more IOL decentration and worse CDVA with CP; Reddy et al likewise reported more decentration with CP than FLACS. In contrast, most studies of posterior capsule opacification (PCO) report a higher incidence after FLACS, possibly because nearby laser treatment induces mesenchymal transformation of lens epithelial cells (LEC), outweighing anticipated benefits from LEC apoptosis near the capsulotomy edge. Pulse energy and duration may influence this response, but PCO subgroup analyses comparing high- and low-energy FLACS are almost nonexistent. Reported Nd: YAG capsulotomy rates are nevertheless lower after FLACS than CP; lower PCO grade and a smaller effect on acuity might explain this, but most publications do not provide grading. Mean absolute error (MAE) is another measure of refractive predictability. Reviews and meta-analyses do not establish a consistent FLACS advantage for postoperative SE: large reviews of randomized control trials (RCTs) suggest greater short-term but not long-term predictability, reviews containing few RCTs report better FLACS MAE at 12 months follow-up, and other systematic reviews combining prospective and retrospective trials find a clinically important MAE difference only at 1 month to 3 months follow-up. Surgically induced astigmatism (SIA) arises during healing at the corneal incision and is particularly relevant to toric IOL implantation. Differences between techniques appear clinically important for SIA predictability, measured as achieved versus attempted correction, but not statistically significant for overall SIA magnitude.

document_sections.heading: Other Surgical Outcomes
document_sections.content: Frequently evaluated operative measures include effective phacoemulsification time (EPT), CDE, and capsulotomy circularity. EPT expresses phacoemulsification time at 100% power in continuous mode. CDE is described as EPT in seconds divided by 6000, or EPT in minutes divided by 100. The authors describe sufficient evidence favoring FLACS over CP on each measure. FLACS produces a more precise, reproducible circular capsulotomy, supporting IOL centration and reducing the risk of malposition; this may improve optical performance.

document_sections.heading: Patient Reported Outcomes
document_sections.content: Evidence on patient-reported outcomes (PROs) is very limited. Differences in how studies assess satisfaction and other subjective outcomes make overall comparison of FLACS with CP difficult, and patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) vary considerably. Because refractive cataract and lens procedures are increasingly common and elective, patient perspectives are important when selecting a suitable premium IOL. More comprehensive, standardized PROMs are needed for rigorous assessment.

document_sections.heading: Complications
document_sections.content: FLACS complications can occur during or after surgery. Typical intraoperative events include suction loss, subconjunctival hemorrhage, and capsule- or pupil-related problems. Suction can fail because of interface defects, patient movement, anatomical features, or conjunctival chemosis; commonly relevant anatomical conditions include conjunctivochalasis, pinguecula, pterygia, and filtration blebs. Some platforms provide different suction-ring diameters to improve docking. Laser delivery should stop immediately after suction loss to prevent inappropriate treatment. Subconjunctival hemorrhage relates to vacuum, treatment duration, and interface type and is more frequent with applanation than with a liquid interface. Posterior capsule rupture (PCR) has been reported less often with FLACS than CP. Reported anterior capsular tears or tags after FLACS vary from 0.1% to as high as 4% and are associated mainly with high-energy platforms. Their more irregular, notched capsulotomy edges may explain this association; the very low anterior capsule complication incidence with low-energy FLACS is comparable to CP. In overall FLACS–CP comparisons, the consequences of capsule-related complications, including a need for vitreoretinal intervention or effects on vision, do not appear statistically significant. They remain consequential for premium IOL implantation, where capsular integrity and optimal centration are essential. Comparative literature addressing low-energy FLACS and CP specifically in this refractive subgroup is scarce. Laser-induced pupil constriction is commonly reported and is associated with prostaglandin release during anterior capsule treatment. It can seriously compromise cataract surgery. Preoperative non-steroid anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are commonly used to help preserve dilation but are normally insufficient by themselves to prevent FLACS-associated miosis; additional approaches may be used individually or together. Attention to laser conditions is also recommended, including a distance of >1 mm between the intended capsulotomy edge and pupil margin and consideration of treatment duration. Most publications do not distinguish pulse-energy types. Recent studies find no laser-induced miosis with low-energy FLACS; the few reviews with a low-energy subgroup report virtually null incidence, comparable to CP. High-pulse energy FLACS, conversely, is associated with constriction almost universally. Postoperative studies have assessed corneal endothelium and retina. Recent adequately powered randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in normal eyes do not show a statistically significant difference in endothelial outcomes, whereas several reviews and meta-analyses report less endothelial cell loss (ECL) after FLACS than CP. Laser fragmentation reduces phacoemulsification time, irrigation volume, and EPT, especially in harder cataracts, which may reduce ECL. Some studies also support endothelial protection in corneal dystrophies such as Fuchs’. Most systematic reviews and meta-analyses find no significant difference in cystoid macular edema (CME). Total macular volume, foveal thickness, and outer macular ring measurements are generally similar, although some studies in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) reported lower central macular volume with FLACS shortly after surgery. FLACS may benefit eyes with macular vulnerability; evidence that ultrasound energy produces a stronger posterior-segment inflammatory response also supports this possibility. FLACS has a substantial learning curve, estimated at a minimum of 100–200 cases according to surgeon experience; most studies report a significant fall in intraoperative complications after that threshold.

document_sections.heading: Indications and Contraindications Indications
document_sections.content: FLACS has been advocated for refractive cataract or lens procedures involving premium IOLs because its customizable, precise, reproducible capsulotomy can improve the centration needed for their performance. FSAK can address low-to-moderate astigmatism. Hard or dense cataracts may favor FLACS: nucleus fragmentation lowers total phacoemulsification time, EPT, and CDE and may reduce endothelial loss. Potential complex-case indications include traumatic subluxated cataracts, zonular instability, intumescent cataracts, and pseudoexfoliation syndrome. Reduced stress on zonules and the posterior capsule may lower postoperative complications. Cataract grade can inform the choice between FLACS and CP; reduced EPT or CDE in hard cataracts may hasten visual recovery. Shallow anterior chambers may likewise benefit. Reports of less endothelial cell loss suggest a possible role in Fuchs’ dystrophy and other endothelial degenerations. FSL can enlarge an anterior capsulotomy to the desired size in capsular contraction syndrome. Recent evidence that low-energy FLACS does not characteristically cause the pupil constriction historically attributed to FLACS is important for the subsequent surgical steps.

document_sections.heading: Contraindications
document_sections.content: Docking may be infeasible with a deep-set globe, narrow palpebral fissure, prominent nose or brow, or inability to lie supine; these are contraindications for FLACS. Conditions that impede anterior-segment OCT or equivalent imaging are also major contraindications, including prior corneal additive surgery with a ring or inlay implant, severe corneal opacity, and edema. Relative contraindications or added challenges include poor dilation (<6 mm diameter), prior keratoplasty or other corneal surgery, glaucoma surgery, white cataracts, mild corneal scarring, and edema. Approaches to inadequate preoperative dilation include topical phenylephrine, cyclopentolate, atropine, and/or NSAIDs given under different preoperative schedules; intracameral epinephrine or phenylephrine; viscomydriasis using viscoelastic; and iris expansion devices. The additional difficulty depends on pulse energy: high-energy FLACS can further constrict an already small pupil, whereas low-energy FLACS reportedly does not require dilation measures beyond those used with CP. Lens fragmentation is not advised for white cataracts because opaque tissue cannot be imaged adequately; variation in water content in white or brunescent cataracts also alters laser-energy absorption. In systems that fragment after capsulotomy, decompression of an intumescent cataract can change posterior capsule depth and increase rupture risk. This sequence-related issue does not apply to systems that fragment before capsulotomy. Corneal scars or edema may prevent complete capsulotomy or fragmentation, although isolated successful FLACS cases have been reported; opacity severity matters. Pterygium, pinguecula, filtration blebs, and glaucoma drainage tubes complicate treatment but should not automatically be absolute contraindications: successful cases have been reported with additional care. Docking can raise intraocular pressure, more so with applanation than with a liquid interface. Nevertheless, evidence has not shown progression of well-controlled glaucoma or other optic neuropathies from this effect.

document_sections.heading: Cost-Effectiveness
document_sections.content: Despite its efficacy and safety in major surgical steps, FLACS currently costs more and is less cost-effective than CP because of platform purchase and consumables. It cannot entirely replace a phacoemulsification/aspiration device, which remains necessary to aspirate lens material and polish the capsular bag. Attempts to lessen dependence on phacoemulsification machines in low-grade cataract or refractive lens surgery reflect the possible value of FLACS precision and capsulotomy customization for premium IOL positioning.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: Evidence of a low anterior capsule complication rate and near absence of laser-induced miosis with low-energy FLACS, comparable to CP, challenges disadvantages historically attributed to FLACS without distinguishing pulse energies. Taking those differences into account, the authors judge FLACS non-inferior to CP for complications and adverse events. They also identify evidence that it can be safer in demanding cases, including corneal dystrophies, lens subluxation, zonular instability such as pseudoexfoliation or Marfan syndrome, harder cataracts, and macular vulnerability. Some evidence favors FLACS for medium-term visual outcomes. Greater precision and customization could be particularly valuable in toric or presbyopia lens surgery, but most published studies lack subgroup analyses by implanted IOL type. Surgery can take longer because most platforms require transfer from the laser to the surgical bed or operating room; a portable platform avoids that transfer and permits surgical durations comparable to CP. FLACS presently cannot match CP on cost-effectiveness because laser equipment and consumables are expensive. CP therefore remains the standard cataract technique, while FLACS is an additional option chiefly for the indications described, usually at extra patient expense. Its costs could change with demand and further improvements. Differences between low- and high-energy pulse systems are becoming clearer but remain infrequently published; understanding them can improve surgical planning. Technological development has broadened and refined FLACS applications, including surgical steps, pulse-energy choices, and portability. The authors consider its complication and adverse-event rates similar to CP when pulse-pattern differences are recognized and suggest it can be a first option in eyes with comorbidities. Broader, better-defined indications may affect use and costs. Further technical advances and larger comparisons of laser systems are needed.
